Mr. Speaker, I found myself in general agreement with the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) this afternoon when he was advocating a national highway. I would not want it to be

National Highways-Mr. Cahill
thought in the house or anywhere else that I was not favourable to the construction of good road's generally. But while I agreed with the hon. member for Bow River in advocating a national highway, I could not sgree with him in his conclusion to vote for the resolution, because it would not bring about the desired end. I am not any more in favour of the amendment except in a general way, than I would be of the resolution. Ordinarily, legislation that is created out of a discussion in the house in a hurry, through an amendment, is not very good legislation. The people generally throughout Canada would, I think, be very glad to see a national highway constructed from ocean to ocean and I think the government would be just as agreeable to that as any person in the country. It would be the means of opening up a great prospect to our Canadian citizens. If our people in the east who are now emigrating had an opportunity of driving their cars through to the west, they might find in the west opportunities that would be of as great advantage to them as they might find by leaving the country. A national highway would be one of the greatest assets, after the construction of our railways, that we could have.
But I do not agree in a general way with the sop handed to the provinces. I think it was the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Clark) who said this afternoon that the principle had been adopted by parliament. My recollection of the matter is that in 1919 the party sitting to the right of the Speaker to-day were unanimously opposed to that resolution granting $20,000,000 as aid to highways throughout the provinces, and I will take the same ground to-day. The aid that was then granted was spent by the provinces on short roads varying from a mile to five, ten or twenty miles in length throughout the various provinces. That is not I think, the object of the people of Canada. What they want, what they would agree to, would be a national highway built on 3ome basis of cooperation between the provincial governments and the Dominion government. I cannot quite agree with the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Dunning) that this road would have to be maintained or operated by the federal government. If there were cooperation in the construction, with an understanding that the provincial governments would maintain the ro<ad as they are now maintaining their highways, we would secure the desired results without having the federal authority in any way conflicting with the provincial authorities.
I would be sorry to see a vote on this resolution. I think we are generally unanimous
[Mr. Cahill.)
in our opinion that a national highway would be beneficial to the country. Many members of parliament would support a special grant towards the construction of such a highway, but it has not been the policy of this party in the past, in my experience, to hand sops to the provinces. Most of those were originated by my hon. friends opposite and they may have Whatever glory may come from them.

Believing that at this time highways are needed in Canada perhaps more than heretofore because means of communication are essential to the welfare of any country, I am in favour of the government granting to the provinces a subsidy to be used for the construction of roads that would make it easier particularly for those on the land, who are making practically the national income, to market their produce. I am not in favour at the present time of a Canadian national highway. Our railways are just beginning to pay their way and a national highway, as things stand at present, would interfere with their earnings. I believe the need of the country, particularly in western Canada, where there are no road materials any better than sand, gravel and clay, is a subsidy for the construction of roads into the outlying districts of those provinces, roads which would feed our railways. I believe that is'the only reasonable attitude for the government to take. We need that; the settlers need it, and it would help the railways to increase their earnings.
I have sometimes thought the whole of the carrying trade should somehow be placed under one great corporation. Where railways are not warranted, a highway is sometimes a necessity, and provincial highways should be constructed in conjunction with the national system of railways to give means of access to all parts of the country. A national highway

National Highways-Mr. Evans
will serve only a particular class, namely the tourists who come here for a little while in the summer. Tourists who come from the United States will not want to go from east to west in our country; they will want to go north into the wilds in order to enjoy themselves in that bracing air and amuse themselves by fishing and so on. There is a need for highways in the provinces and I hope the government will see fit to grant a subsidy for that purpose.

speechtext:
I rise to give my support to this
resolution, coming as I do from one of the great tourist sections of Canada which is intimately connected with good roads and which has seen more or less the financial benefit that follows a system of this kind. I support the resolution on another ground, that advanced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in the house the other day when he said that it was the duty of government to increase the happiness, contentment and prosperity of our people. Looking at rural Canada, I know nothing that will contribute more to the peace, happiness and prosperity of the people than three things. First, good roads, which has been the subject of debate here this afternoon and on previous occasions. Second, rural telephones, which puts one neighbour in contact almost every minute of the day with his friends and neighbours. Third, rural mail delivery, the task which has been committed to my hon. friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Veniot), and I would like to take this opportunity of thanking him publicly in this house for being considerate of the requests which I have made of him. I might also inform him that it is my intention to come to him again with more and even greater requests than I have made of him in the past, and I expect to be met by that genial smile and that cordial welcome which he has always accorded me in the past. Consequently, with these three ends in view, which I think will increase the happiness, content and prosperity of the people of rural Canada, I have very much pleasure indeed in supporting the resolution.
I cannot possibly agree with the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning), and I am very much surprised that one who, coming to this house with such a reputation as he had, has .failed to grasp the significance of a resolution of this kind. He hides behind that old excuse which is so often trotted out in this house, the British North America Act. I could not help but agree for once in my life, and I did it with considerable diffidence, with my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) when he said that the British North America Act might yet sound the deathknell of confederation. I should be very sorry to see that, because I realize that the British North America Act is the backbone of our constitution and one of the safeguards of our people. But who sixty years ago could forecast the conditions that we have in this country to-day? As my hon. friend from Ontario (Mr. Kaiser) has pointed out, the automobile industry was not in existence at that time, and when the great burden was placed upon the provinces of building and maintaining the roads of this country, I am sure it could not possibly have been conceived at that time what a great burden this would ultimately become. In fact, I am one of those who believe that that burden is too great to-day for any province in the Dominion to carry successfully, and too great a task for the provinces to undertake in the manner it ought to be undertaken in the interests of the people.
Moreover, this government has in the past, as no doubt it will in the future, invaded the revenue-producing fields of the provinces. The federal government has, for instance, tapped the income tax field, which rightly belongs to the provinces, while at the same time the provinces have no new sources of revenue to tap to meet their burdens, which are daily becoming greater until to-day they are almost unbearable. Consequently I say the time has come-and if it has not come now it certainly will be reached in the very near future-when the Dominion government should come to the assistance of the provinces in carrying on these great works, which, after all, are in the interests of the citizens of all Canada.
I support this resolution for another reason. I support it on business grounds. When we look back and see how a business that ten years ago amounted to nothing is contributing to-day at least $25,000,000 to the exchequer of Canada, and distributing among the pockets of our people $276,000,000 a year, thereby increasing their prosperity, we do not need to have very much vision to realize that in the not distant future, possibly within the next ten years, that business will double and treble and quadruple, so that the revenue received by the exchequer will amount, not merely to $25,000,000, but probably $50,000,000 or $75,000,000. I submit that no business man and no business institution whose business was growing to the extent I have indicated would hesitate to lay plans for the enlargement of plant to take care of that greater business which there was every reason to anticipate.

National Highways[DOT]-Mr. McGibbon
From that point of view therefore it is good business for the government to support this resolution and to spend, not merely $10,000,000 or $20,000,000, but $30,000,000 or $40,000,000 on the building of good roads, spread over the next ten or fifteen years.
I support this resolution also on national grounds. As has been stated here this afternoon, with greater facilities for communication established between east and west there will develop a greater national spirit and harmony in this country, producing a more contented and a happier people.
I support the resolution for still another reason. We know that to-day one of our great problems is that if immigration, and we know also from our experience in the past that one of the difficulties in connection with immigration has been the finding of employment for those who come here. As we look back over our history we find that the most prosperous years we have had from an immigration standpoint have been almost invariably associated with some nation-wide work, such as railway building, which provides employment for the new settlers in the off season of the year and enabled them to make money enough during the dull season to carry them over their first few years in this country. This national highway scheme would provide employment for our immigrants at certain seasons of the year.
I also support this resolution in the light of history. We know that many of the countries of the world that are most prosperous to-day were in difficulties some years ago. I have been told by natives of the state of California, for instance, that before the tourist traffic was developed that state was so poor that it was almost on the point of bankruptcy. But now, with the enormous increase in tourist traffic to that state, it is one of the most prosperous in the union.
There is still another reason why I support this resolution. We are living alongside one of the big countries of the world, a country with 110,000,000 people, a country with which we are in constant communication, a country to which we owe some $2,500,000,000. I submit, as was pointed out by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) the other day, that the revenue to be derived from the tourist trade will help to keep the Canadian dollar at par, and to maintain our balance of trade at the favourable point it is at to-day; and furthermore, the more Americans we have come to this country, and the more they 
intermingle with Canadians and the more Canadians intermingle with them, so much better will be the spirit of goodwill existing between the two nations, a consideration which is so essential to our national life and to our prosperity.
I have enumerated only a few of the reasons, Mr. Speaker, why I support the resolution of the hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Kellner), who I think deserves the thanks of this house for bringing this matter to the attention of parliament. If this resolution is not voted on and carried into effect at this time, I have no hesitation in saying that in the not very distant future this government will have to take up the burden of developing a national highway system in the Dominion of Canada. That is necessary in order that Canadians may know their country, in order that they may know each other, and in order that they may be prosperous.
The Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) appeared to be very anxious to raise objections to this resolution. Of course you can raise objections to any proposal; but I submit it is the duty of governments to overcome difficulties, not to create them, especially when it is in the interests of the people that those difficulties should be overcome. I cannot treat some of his objections seriously. For instance, I cannot conceive it possible that, say, the province of Ontario would turn down a grant from the federal treasury to build roads, even though there were strings attached to it, for such a grant would in turn relieve the province of certain obligations. The only legitimate objection that occurs to me is that the government responsible for raising money should be responsible for spending it. That objection, however, has not been raised either by the government or by any of its supporters.
A good proportion iof the memhers to your right, Mr. Speaker, come from rural ridings where roads are almost as essential as daily bread, and to me it is an interesting sight to watch them sitting there and allowing themselves to be led by the Minister of Railways practically in silence to oppose this resolution. I think I can speak with a good deal of confidence when I say that not one of those members represents the opinions of the people who sent him to this house.
